h.select_rule: Choose hypotheses with a clear causal mechanism, a large expected change in the edit's effect, and support from retrieved evidence or well-established principles such as diminishing returns, redundancy, or bottlenecks. Reject any whose direction hinges on subtle trade-offs.
h.strategy: Use retrieved findings about which components interact and which are redundant or critical. Build hypotheses around robust interaction patterns: an edit has less effect when its target is bypassed or redundant, and more effect when its target is the only or limiting pathway. Removal effects are stronger when there is little remaining alternative capacity. Propose diverse hypotheses across different edit types and conditions, each with a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: Edge 0 gates all paths through node 1, so enabling it with a conv unlocks much more computation than upgrading an existing op.
Adding a conv where the edge was absent contributes new capacity, whereas replacing an existing op yields a smaller delta.
Connecting node 1 to node 2 with a conv adds depth and feature mixing that was previously missing.
Restoring a removed edge with a conv adds a learnable path into the output node.
Filling a missing output-feeding edge with a conv adds capacity to a limiting pathway.
Removing a conv from the first edge destroys more capacity than removing a weak op like pooling or none.
Deleting a conv on a final-node edge loses more learned capacity than deleting a parameter-free op.
Removing a conv edge into the output is costlier than removing a pool or skip edge.
Without the direct 0-to-3 edge, edge 0 is a limiting route, so removing it is more harmful.
With no direct input-to-output edge, removing edge 5 cuts off more of the remaining signal flow.
